The fix — whether you are proposing one, writing the patch, or revising an existing one — must be **durable** and **well-researched**, and must **address the root cause**. Be unapologetically critical about fix quality: it is far better to spend extra time now and fix the flakiness for good than to whip up a lightly researched patch. Spending time learning the feature under test and the surrounding code (application and test) is expected and encouraged.

Most of this is judgment, and a justified departure is fine. The items under **Don't hide the failure** are not judgment calls: a patch that needs one of them isn't a fix. A departure from either the best practices below or this document must be justified in the PR description (not in code comments; a good fix is self-explanatory).

Again, be unapologetically critical about the fix quality.

#### Testing best practices

Read these even when the surrounding test file predates them. They won't cover every scenario.

- [`scout-best-practices.md`](/docs/extend/testing/scout-best-practices.md) — shared Scout rules: pick the right test type, tolerate leftover data, and don't leak state.
- [`ui-best-practices.md`](/docs/extend/testing/ui-best-practices.md) — Scout UI: wait on the rendered result, prefer APIs for setup, and avoid retry loops and hard sleeps.
- [`api-best-practices.md`](/docs/extend/testing/api-best-practices.md) — Scout API: call the endpoint under test with `apiClient`, and assert status plus response shape.

#### What a good fix looks like

- **Fix the cause, where it lives.** A product bug or a wrong assertion is the preferred fix over any test-side workaround. For UI tests, addressing the root cause often means surfacing state in the DOM so the test can wait on a real readiness signal instead of guessing. This is the most important item in this entire section. DO take every effort to expose state in the DOM itself so tests have reliable readiness signals.
- **A test-side wait can't fix a production-side race.** If the evidence points to a race in product code, adding `await` / `waitFor` in the test only makes the test wait longer — the race is still there for users. This is the most common pattern that looks like a fix but isn't. Fix the race.
- **Be skeptical of nearby code** The codebase is old and some anti-patterns have accumulated; don't copy a retry or a wait from a neighboring test just because it is there. At the same time, an existing block retrying interactions in a long-lived test may be there for a reason — check the file history before removing it.
- **Shared code has a wide blast radius.** A change to a shared page object, fixture, service, or framework package (`kbn-test*`, `kbn-ftr-*`, `@kbn/scout*`) affects every suite that uses it, so verify it more broadly than the one failing spec.
- **A green flaky-runner result, when applicable, is necessary, not sufficient.** A patch that tolerates or retries away the failure passes every run precisely because it hides the cause, and the runner cannot reproduce Cloud pipelines or the neighboring configs that share test servers. Ask whether the fix would still hold if the underlying cause fired.
- **It is OK not to have a fix.** Some failures are infrastructure-related and outside your control, and some can't be diagnosed with the data at hand. Saying so — and naming what information would settle it — is a better outcome than a speculative patch.

#### Retries, waits, and timeouts

- **Retries hide bugs more often than they fix them.** We generally discourage `retry` blocks: retrying an interaction hides an actionability bug a real user would hit (an element off-screen, the wrong sub-element targeted, an unstable re-render), and re-running an action re-fires its side effects. A retry can be acceptable when it works around a framework timing limitation rather than application behavior, or when the triggering action is inside the retried block _and_ re-running it has no side effects (in case it fired before the page was ready to react).
- **Re-running a read is a wait; re-running an action is not.** Polling a _read_ — a bounded poll that evaluates a value or condition and settles when it matches (web-first assertions, `expect.poll` / `toPass`, `retry.waitForWithTimeout` on a boolean) — is a legitimate wait, as long as it targets the right observable signal and re-queries inside the loop (a handle captured once goes stale). What hides bugs is re-running an _action_ (`click`, type, `goto`, an HTTP call) — or any retried block that re-fires side effects — unless it falls under the exception above. A framework poll that only re-evaluates a read counts as a wait even though it retries on a thrown assertion (`toPass` works that way); a hand-rolled retry around a throwing read is not banned outright, but it is better expressed as one bounded wait (see "Give a wait one owner" below).
- **A wait should target a concrete observable signal** — an element, an attribute, a request completing. Waiting for the sake of it, or hoping a delay makes the flake go away, isn't a well-researched fix. A fixed sleep (`page.waitForTimeout`, `sleep`, a `setTimeout`-based delay) is the clearest case: the delay that passes locally is the one that fails under CI load.
- **Wait on the signal the failing assertion reads, not an earlier step.** Guarding the click (`{ force: true }`, a retry), dismissing a toast, or waiting on a spinner while the element the assertion reads still races is the most common way a wait-based fix silently fails. Identify which step produced the reported error and wait on that.
- **Prefer a DOM signal over a global indicator or a network wait.** Don't rely on a global loading indicator (e.g. the Kibana chrome spinner) to tell you a specific piece of UI has loaded. Look for a way to surface the state on the application side instead (a `data-test-subj`, a `data-loaded` attribute, a state marker): it reflects the committed render and survives endpoint changes. If a network wait is the only option, arm `page.waitForResponse(...)` _before_ the action that triggers the request, and remember that a resolved response doesn't mean the DOM has updated — and when the app fires several requests to the same endpoint, the wait can match the wrong one.
- **Prefer removing the race over waiting it out.** Put the preconditions in place before the flow runs — mock a gating endpoint, ingest data via API before logging in — rather than waiting on a nondeterministic arrival. As the best practices note, set up data with API helpers instead of clicking through the UI, which is slower and more prone to flakiness.
- **Give a wait one owner.** Nesting an outer retry around a helper that already waits (`retry.tryForTime(20_000, () => existOrFail(x, { timeout: 5_000 }))`) makes the effective budget unclear — a `tryForTime` deadline is checked between attempts, not during one — so prefer a single direct bounded wait (`existOrFail(x, { timeout: 20_000 })`).
- **A timeout bump shouldn't be the go-to fix.** It makes the test pass without explaining what was slow. Investigate what never happened: is the slow operation intrinsic to the product (e.g. index creation, a scheduled task), a missing wait upstream, or a product defect? If a bump is still the right call, justify it in the PR description and raise it well past the slowest run you observed — a one-second bump only moves the edge. (A slow Jest render is the one place a bump is a genuine fix; see below.)

#### Don't hide the failure

- **Don't reduce coverage to make the failure go away.** Skipping the test (`describe.skip` / `it.skip`), stripping deployment tags, or excluding it from an environment because "it's flaky there" hides whatever the test was catching. Excluding it is legitimate only when there is documented evidence that the environment doesn't support what the test exercises — do the research and explain why.
- **Don't bend the assertion or the product to the test.** Loosening an assertion, narrowing its scope, or changing product code just so the assertion passes hides what the test was catching. Correcting the assertion is different: when it expects something the product never promised (a fixed order, an exact count in a shared environment), the assertion is the bug and replacing it with the right expectation is the fix.
- **Tolerating an expected error is fine when it is a correctness fix.** Making teardown idempotent — e.g. tolerating a 404 when deleting a resource that may not exist — is legitimate. Swallowing errors so a flaky step passes is not.
- **Fix the framework through its documented interface.** Framework fixes (Scout, FTR, shared page objects and fixtures) are welcome, but don't work around the framework: don't widen a framework package's public surface or export internals to enable a fix, and stick to documented features (e.g. the documented tagging mechanisms). Developer-experience improvements the framework could make are worth noting in the PR description.

#### Recognizing patterns

- **Passes locally and alone, fails in CI: suspect shared state first.** Other suites and parallel workers run against the same test servers and leave data behind, and Cloud deployments ship with content a local stack doesn't have. Check what state the failing assertion depends on and who else could create or delete it — fixed resource names, fixed time windows, position-based selection, or asserting that data is _absent_ are the usual culprits (`scout-best-practices.md`: "Expect a shared test environment", "Don't leak state into the next suite"). A wait is the wrong tool for this class.
- **A stale or empty read after a write is a propagation problem — diagnose who owns it before calling it "environment".** When a readiness signal is satisfied but a later read returns stale or empty (a config poll, cache, ES refresh, entity-store or cluster sync, multi-node lag), a bigger timeout only hides it. Ask which of three it is: **(1)** a convergence signal exists and the test isn't using it → wait on that signal (index with `refresh=wait_for`, poll the _read_); **(2)** no such signal exists → an application _observability gap_, so propose exposing one (an event, status field, or endpoint) rather than looping in the test; **(3)** the product returns stale, or errors, where it should be read-your-writes consistent (a cache not invalidated after a write, a transient "unknown index" surfaced to the user) → an **application bug the test correctly caught**, so fix the product. When classifying, reserve `test-environment` for shared-environment interference and `ci-environment` for a demonstrated CI/infrastructure cause — not for the product's own convergence behavior, which is (1), (2), or (3).
- **A recurrence at a different step is a new flake, not proof the last fix was wrong.** The same test may have been patched before, by an engineer or by automation. If the original failure signature stopped and the test now races at a _different_ step, the original fix likely held — treat the new step as its own flake and apply the same readiness thinking to it. If fresh races keep surfacing at successive steps, the test probably drives too much through the UI: prefer collapsing the flow (establish state via API, or split the test) over stacking one wait after another.
- **Parallel load is real, but not a reason to go sequential by default.** Parallel Scout configs put pressure on the shared test servers, so factor that load into the diagnosis. If a test is genuinely slow under parallel load and a timeout bump doesn't help, moving that spec to a sequential run is an option — but parallel is the default for UI suites, and load alone isn't a reason to drop `workers` or move a whole config.
- **Flaky selectors are a root cause too.** A strict-mode "resolved to N elements" error, `.first()` / `.nth()`, or an unscoped text matcher points at the locator, not at timing — see `ui-best-practices.md`: "Locate UI elements reliably".

#### Jest and React Testing Library

As always, first check for a product bug or a wrong assertion. Beyond that, a Jest/RTL flake is more often a _cost_ problem than a waiting problem: these tests get a 5-second budget unless the file or plugin raises it, and a single `waitFor` / `findBy*` can consume 4.5 seconds of it (`asyncUtilTimeout` in `kbn-test`'s RTL setup), so a render that is slow under CI's parallel load runs out of time. A React "not wrapped in act" warning is another tell — CI silences console output, so you will only see it locally. If your research concludes the failure is a time-budget issue, here are some tips to make the test cheaper:

- Remove the async step so there is nothing to wait for. RTL wraps `fireEvent` in `act`, so a synchronous state update is already applied when it returns and you can read it with `getBy…` on the next line. When the update really waits on a promise or a timer, keep `findBy*` / `waitFor` — the goal is to delete the async step, not to assert across one.
- Render the component already in the state you want to check, instead of clicking your way there.
- Test a smaller unit: one component, a hook, or a plain function, not a whole page.
- Mock every heavy child the test does not assert on. Mocking only some of them usually does not save enough.
- Fix the underlying defect when there is one: a missing `await`, a value that genuinely arrives later so its assertion belongs inside `waitFor`, data that is not deterministic, or a product bug the test exposed.
- We found that leaving the slow render in place and only changing how the test waits for it — swapping the wrapper for a lighter provider while the same component still mounts, or retuning `userEvent` / `act` / `waitFor` such as `delay: null` — usually doesn't hold. Those help only when the render is already cheap. `.agents/skills/enzyme-to-rtl/SKILL.md` covers `fireEvent` versus `userEvent`, mocking heavy EUI children, and fake timers.
- Raising the Jest timeout is a last resort, but a legitimate one when the render itself is the slow part and you cannot cut its cost without dropping what the test checks — there is no earlier signal a wait could reach. Raise it for the test (`it(…, ms)`), the file (`jest.setTimeout(ms)`), or the plugin (`testTimeout` in its `jest.config.js`), and clear the slowest run you measured by a wide margin. Raise the Jest timeout, never the `waitFor` / `findBy*` timeout: waiting longer on a slow render buys nothing.
